what_it_does: When a chip is being designed, software tools called logic synthesizers transform a high-level circuit description into a network of logic gates. Different parts of a circuit respond better to different optimization tricks, but figuring out which trick to apply where is expensive because it requires actually running the optimizer and measuring the result. This paper proposes a method that first groups circuit regions by their structural fingerprints — patterns learned from the local wiring around each gate — so that similar regions receive the same optimization technique without needing to simulate every option individually. A self-supervised machine-learning model (one that trains itself using the circuit's own structure rather than hand-labeled data) is used to predict those fingerprints cheaply, cutting down the cost of deciding which optimizer to apply where. The approach is described as 'late breaking results,' meaning it is a preliminary finding rather than a fully evaluated system.
